title: Shared-state composition across MPC, FHE, and proofs
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Develop a checked construction discipline for services that reuse commitments, authentication keys, FHE keys, or randomness across concurrent MPC and proof sessions, without recompiling the entire service into generic MPC.
status: Design target; UC composition is established, but a particular implementation must satisfy its shared-state and interface requirements.
why: Prevents individually secure components from creating an insecure combined service.
key_works: Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security: A New Paradigm for Cryptographic Protocols*, ePrint 2000/067.

title: Security degradation with multiple corruption thresholds
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Specify protocols that retain different guarantees—privacy, public correctness, attributable abort, availability—at different corruption levels, with provably safe transitions between operating modes.
status: Frontier combination; publicly auditable MPC already separates correctness from confidentiality under stronger corruption.
why: Replaces a single catastrophic trust threshold with useful residual guarantees.
key_works: Kanjalkar, Zhang, Gandlur, and Miller (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service with succinct verification and universal setup*, arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Adaptive security for the complete service lifecycle
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Prove adaptive security across enrollment, DKG, preprocessing, evaluation, proving, output release, refresh, and recovery under one corruption model.
status: Design target; erasure-free adaptive UC DKG exists, but does not automatically establish adaptive security of downstream components.
why: Protects services against compromise occurring during operation rather than only before initialization.
key_works: Ek, Melissaris, and Roy (2026), *Adaptively Secure, Universally Composable Distributed Generation of Discrete-Logarithm Based Keys*, ePrint 2026/457.

title: Whole-stack post-quantum security
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Build an auditable private-computation service whose transport, authentication, DKG, encryption, commitments, proofs, and recovery all satisfy a compatible post-quantum security definition.
status: Design target; post-quantum collaborative proofs and lattice-based asynchronous DKG provide substantial components.
why: Eliminates classical auxiliary primitives that silently defeat a post-quantum claim.
key_works: Pappas, Papadopoulos, and Papamanthou (2026), *Code-based Scalable Collaborative SNARKs*, ePrint 2026/729; Yang et al. (2025), *Robust and Scalable Lattice-Based Distributed Key Generation for Asynchronous Networks*, ePrint 2025/1946.

title: Lifetime leakage from aborts and retries
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Establish a composable privacy accountant covering successful outputs, selective aborts, rejected inputs, retries, and error messages throughout a service’s lifetime.
status: Frontier; 2026 work quantifies important abort effects for differential privacy, but broader mixed-stack leakage accounting remains a separate target.
why: Prevents repeated execution from becoming an extraction oracle.
key_works: Meisingseth (2026), *On Aborts in Differential Privacy*, ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Correlation-aware committee security
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Optimize committee selection using correlated operator, cloud, software, jurisdictional, and recovery failures rather than treating every participant as an independent trust domain.
status: Evidence and modeling target; threshold specifications identify cryptographic parties, not empirical independence of their operators.
why: Makes “distributed trust” correspond to actual failure diversity.
key_works: NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, NIST IR 8214C, DOI:10.6028/NIST.IR.8214C.

title: Semantics-preserving mixed-arithmetic compilation
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Automatically certify conversions between modular integers, fixed-point values, approximate real arithmetic, and Boolean representations while preserving both security and application semantics.
status: Design frontier; mixed-protocol frameworks exist, but numerical meaning and corruption guarantees must survive every conversion.
why: Prevents fast hybrid implementations from computing the wrong function securely.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Public auditing of private programs
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Publicly verify execution of a committed program while hiding its sensitive structure, including branches, policy rules, model architecture, and data-dependent resource use.
status: Design target; public auditing is established, but hiding the relation and its operational footprint adds separate requirements.
why: Enables auditability without disclosing proprietary algorithms.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service*, arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Everlasting privacy with durable public accountability
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Construct practical distributed computation whose audit records remain statistically private after computational assumptions fail, while retaining useful public accountability.
status: Frontier combination; computationally private succinct audit systems provide a baseline, not automatically everlasting privacy.
why: Protects sensitive records that must remain confidential for decades.
key_works: Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security*, ePrint 2000/067; Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Proving inclusion of every accepted input
open: Prove that every submission acknowledged before a cutoff was included exactly once, while hiding its value and unnecessary participant metadata.
status: Design target; correctness over committed inputs does not alone establish completeness of the admission process.
why: Prevents selective censorship disguised as valid computation.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service*, arXiv:2107.04248; Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Authenticated inputs under dishonest-majority public blame
open: Preserve the efficiency of authenticated-input MPC while supporting dishonest-majority computation and compact public evidence identifying invalid authentication or inconsistent sharing.
status: Frontier extension; the cited authenticated-input compiler provides honest-majority constructions and identifiable-abort guarantees in specified thresholds.
why: Connects institutional credentials to stronger outsourced-computation models.
key_works: Dutta, Ganesh, Patranabis, and Singh (2024), *Compute, but Verify: Efficient Multiparty Computation over Authenticated Inputs*, ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Auditable authorization-policy versions
open: Bind each private execution to the policy version actually authorized at admission, including revocation, expiry, and changes occurring before output release.
status: Design target; authenticated data and correct execution do not automatically prove that the execution was authorized.
why: Prevents stale or mismatched permissions from producing valid but unauthorized results.
key_works: Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Incrementally auditable reactive MPC
open: Maintain one succinct public proof over a continuing MPC service, binding admitted inputs, state transitions, outputs, and code versions without replaying its entire history.
status: Design frontier; collaborative incremental verification exists, but a complete reactive service has additional admission and state-continuity obligations.
why: Makes years of private computation publicly checkable.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410.

title: Audit generation that is safe on invalid witnesses
open: Ensure malformed distributed inputs cannot cause an audit prover to leak honest participants’ secrets before it rejects or aborts.
status: Frontier hardening problem; 2025 work shows that collaborative proving can require more care than running a prover inside malicious MPC.
why: Protects privacy precisely when adversaries violate the intended relation.
key_works: Garg, Goel, Jain, Roberts, and Sekar (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026.

title: Non-equivocating private audit histories
open: Prevent a service from presenting mutually inconsistent valid histories to different auditors, while allowing selective disclosure and intermittently connected clients.
status: Design target; a valid proof of one history does not establish that it is the unique authoritative history.
why: Prevents hidden double accounting and inconsistent private ledgers.
key_works: Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security*, ePrint 2000/067; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Proof availability after computation completes
open: Preserve the ability to finish a public proof after some participants disappear following successful private computation, without reconstructing the distributed witness.
status: Design target; collaborative proving supplies the privacy mechanism, but proof durability is a distinct completion property.
why: Avoids correct results becoming unusable because their proof was stranded.
key_works: Ozdemir and Boneh (2022), *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs: Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Distributed Secrets*, USENIX Security 2022.

title: Private, verifiable resource billing
open: Produce verifiable bills for MPC, FHE, and proof generation while hiding sensitive program structure, inputs, and utilization patterns.
status: Design target; computation proofs and economic fairness address different parts of the billing problem.
why: Makes outsourced private computation economically auditable.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248; Friolo et al. (2022), *Cryptographic and Financial Fairness*, arXiv:2207.10780.

title: Public auditing below ten-percent overhead
open: Demonstrate public auditability adding less than 10% to total cost over an otherwise identical maliciously secure MPC workload, including proving, storage, communication, and verification.
status: Proposed moonshot, not a published record; succinct verification does not imply cheap proof production.
why: Makes public auditing an ordinary service feature.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service with succinct verification and universal setup*, arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Subsecond proofs of programmable bootstrapping
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Prove a representative TFHE evaluation and programmable bootstrap in under one second at matching security parameters, with public verification and all proving costs included.
status: Proposed performance frontier; HasteBoots reports approximately ten seconds for one evaluation/bootstrap, not the older tens-of-minutes baseline.
why: Makes integrity practical for low-latency encrypted services.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots: Proving TFHE Programmable Bootstrapping in Seconds*, USENIX Security 2026.

title: Bounded-memory proofs for long bootstrap sequences
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Prove sustained TFHE computation with many bootstraps using bounded working memory and incremental checkpoints, without materializing the complete execution trace.
status: Frontier extension; HasteBoots demonstrates batching, including sixteen operations within one minute in its configuration.
why: Supports persistent encrypted programs rather than short benchmark circuits.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots*, USENIX Security 2026; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Simultaneously cheap RNS proving and verification
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Improve the joint prover-time, verifier-time, and proof-size frontier for complete RNS-based HE pipelines, rather than improving one by substantially worsening another.
status: Frontier; PRISM reports approximately 3.5× slower proving than ZHE while improving verification or proof size by up to 7.8×.
why: Avoids moving the verification bottleneck to the service provider.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM: Efficient zkSNARKs for RNS-Based Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Low-cost zero knowledge for lattice-native verifiable FHE
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Match efficient lattice-native FHE verification while additionally hiding server-private inputs and auxiliary execution information under a complete zero-knowledge definition.
status: Frontier combination; verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge verifiable FHE are not interchangeable guarantees.
why: Enables confidential models and policies on untrusted encrypted-computation servers.
key_works: Atapoor et al. (2024), *Verifiable FHE via Lattice-based SNARKs*, DOI:10.62056/a6ksdkp10; Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Cheaper soundness for SIMD transcript packing
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Reduce or prove necessary the additional soundness cost of checking packed verifiable-FHE transcripts, preserving SIMD efficiency against malformed encodings.
status: Frontier sharpened by Laminate’s May 2026 correction: its repaired well-formedness test adds security-parameter-dependent ciphertext overhead.
why: Makes proof compression reliable rather than a new attack surface.
key_works: Peshawaria, Liu, Fisch, and Tromer (2025/2026), *Laminate: Succinct SIMD-Friendly Verifiable FHE*, ePrint 2025/2285.

title: Application-level error certificates for CKKS
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Prove a bound between the decrypted CKKS result and the intended real-number computation, accounting for encoding, approximation, rescaling, rounding, and accumulated error.
status: Frontier extension; proving HE execution does not by itself prove application-level numerical accuracy.
why: Makes encrypted scientific and financial results interpretable.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proofs for HE Evaluations*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Proof compatibility with optimized FFT implementations
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Certify equivalence between production floating-point FFT-based FHE kernels and proof-friendly exact NTT representations, including approximation and overflow conditions.
status: Engineering frontier; HasteBoots explains the arithmetic mismatch and uses proof-friendly quotient-ring representations.
why: Avoids maintaining a slow “provable” implementation separate from the fast production one.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots*, USENIX Security 2026.

title: Hidden-noise decryption-reliability proofs
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Certify a ciphertext’s decryption-failure probability without exposing keys, plaintexts, or an unnecessarily revealing noise trace.
status: Frontier question; execution integrity and reliable decryptability are distinct statements.
why: Prevents evaluators from returning technically evaluated but unusable ciphertexts.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770; Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Proof-bound conditional decryption
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Design a decryption API that releases plaintext only for an authorized evaluation proof, with security covering malicious ciphertexts, proof replay, repeated requests, and errors.
status: Design target; verifiable evaluation must be composed with the actual decryption security model.
why: Prevents a valid-looking proof interface from becoming a key-recovery oracle.
key_works: Colin de Verdière, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *On Threshold Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Synchronized Decryptors*, ePrint 2026/031; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*.

title: Tight costs of strongly simulatable asynchronous decryption
open: Determine tighter communication, modulus, storage, and threshold tradeoffs for strongly simulatable asynchronous threshold FHE, including matching lower bounds where possible.
status: Frontier; the 2026 Shamir-based construction substantially reduces earlier storage and modulus requirements, so older large-overhead baselines are stale.
why: Identifies which threshold-FHE costs are structural.
key_works: Kim, Lee, Lee, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *Asynchronous Shamir-Based Threshold FHE: Smaller Moduli and Strong Simulation Security*, ePrint 2026/973.

title: Robust decryption without a privileged combiner
open: Replace a semi-honest available combiner with a Byzantine-resilient combining service, preserving output delivery under explicitly sufficient honest-participation assumptions.
status: Design extension; MOZI’s advertised output-delivery guarantees distinguish semi-honest and malicious combiners.
why: Removes a centralized availability assumption from distributed decryption.
key_works: Chang et al. (2026), *MOZI: Threshold FHE at Scale: Efficient and Resilient, for Large-Scale MPC*, NIST TCPT3 presentation.

title: Safe adaptive-query threshold-CKKS services
open: Prove security of long-lived threshold-CKKS APIs under adaptive ciphertexts, repeated approximate outputs, precision changes, authorization reuse, and error responses.
status: Design frontier sharpened by 2026 attacks and repaired synchronized-decryptor models.
why: Protects the key across the complete query history.
key_works: Colin de Verdière, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *On Threshold Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Synchronized Decryptors*, ePrint 2026/031.

title: Concurrent authorization of changing decryptor sets
open: Support simultaneous decryption requests assigned to different authorized subsets without allowing shares from separate requests, epochs, or policies to be recombined.
status: Frontier extension; strong designated-decryptor security exists, but concurrent operational authorization requires explicit binding.
why: Makes decryption policy part of the cryptography rather than an administrative convention.
key_works: Colin de Verdière et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/031.

title: Sparse threshold-CKKS DKG under WAN faults
open: Demonstrate sparse-key DKG for at least 1,000 parties with malicious robustness, public verification, realistic WAN transport, and complete setup accounting.
status: Design target; Min et al. report two seconds for computational components on an RTX 4090 through 1,024 parties—not full WAN completion.
why: Preserves efficient CKKS bootstrapping without central key generation.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Refreshable threshold evaluation keys
open: Refresh or replace the distributed authority behind bootstrapping, rotation, and key-switching keys without reconstructing the secret or requiring a complete service outage.
status: Design target; efficient threshold key generation does not alone provide lifecycle management for all derived evaluation keys.
why: Makes threshold FHE maintainable over years.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Recovery with historical ciphertext continuity
open: Recover from permitted operator compromises while retaining authorized access to historical ciphertexts and preventing new committees from inheriting unnecessary historical authority.
status: Design combination; proactive sharing and threshold FHE supply ingredients, but ciphertext continuity adds migration obligations.
why: Avoids abandoning encrypted data after an incident.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), *On the (Im)possibility of Asynchronous Proactive Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2026/2018; Kim et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/973.

title: Short decryption shares with public accountability
open: Preserve compact decryption shares while adding malicious-share rejection, transferable blame, and recovery for arbitrary authorized subsets.
status: Frontier combination; serverless short-share threshold FHE already exists.
why: Keeps accountable decryption practical for bandwidth-constrained participants.
key_works: Okada and Takagi (2026), *Threshold FHE with Short Decryption Shares without a Semi-trusted Server*, ePrint 2026/957; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

title: Threshold FHE within twice single-key lifecycle cost
open: Demonstrate an auditable, maliciously secure threshold-FHE application with total amortized cost below 2× an equivalent single-key implementation, including setup, refresh, and decryption.
status: Proposed moonshot; component-level improvements do not establish this application-level ratio.
why: Makes distributed trust inexpensive enough to adopt routinely.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057; Okada and Takagi (2026), ePrint 2026/957.

title: Concrete fully succinct multi-key FHE
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Implement fully succinct multi-key FHE with defensible concrete parameters and compare total memory, evaluation, and decryption costs against practical nonsuccinct alternatives.
status: Engineering frontier; Afshar–Goyal already achieve leveled LWE-based succinctness of ciphertexts and individual public and secret keys.
why: Tests whether asymptotic compactness translates into usable multi-owner computation.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Bootstrapped fully succinct multi-key services
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Preserve useful multi-key succinctness through practical arbitrary-depth evaluation, accounting for bootstrapping material and all distributed-decryption costs.
status: Frontier extension; the cited fully succinct construction is leveled.
why: Extends compact multi-owner computation beyond a fixed depth budget.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Publicly verifiable near-rate-one multi-key decryption
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Retain amortized decryption communication approaching plaintext size while adding public correctness evidence and malicious-share accountability.
status: Frontier combination; rate-one simulatable partial decryption exists, but extra verification material must be counted.
why: Avoids losing compactness when moving from privacy to accountable operation.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Rivinius (2025), *MPC with Publicly Identifiable Abort from Pseudorandomness and Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2025/258.

title: Owner revocation after multi-key evaluation
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Specify and implement revocation of future use while preserving previously authorized result access, without granting remaining owners unrestricted access to a departed owner’s inputs.
status: Design target; succinct multi-key evaluation does not determine consent or revocation semantics.
why: Supports collaborations whose membership changes.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Auditable admission of adversarial multi-key owners
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Admit independently generated keys while checking ownership, parameter compatibility, and required key relations without introducing a trusted registration authority.
status: Design target; a service must instantiate the key-generation and registration assumptions of its multi-key construction.
why: Prevents malformed or misbound participant keys from breaking collaboration.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; NIST (2026), IR 8214C.

title: Public receipts for FHE-to-share conversion
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Convert ciphertexts into authenticated shares with compact evidence binding the source ciphertext, destination committee, arithmetic interpretation, and authorization.
status: Design target; hybrid HE–MPC systems provide conversion precedents, not a universal publicly verifiable conversion interface.
why: Removes trusted adapters between encrypted and interactive execution.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee: Secure Two-party Inference Framework for Large Transformers*, ePrint 2023/1678; Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*.

title: Verifiable switching between approximate, exact, and Boolean computation
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Switch among CKKS, exact modular arithmetic, and Boolean computation while proving range, rounding, and value-preservation conditions under distributed key custody.
status: Design frontier; mixed computation exists, but each conversion’s semantic and cryptographic preconditions must be composed.
why: Lets applications use the most efficient representation for each operation.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Leakage-aware hybrid optimization
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Optimize representation choices, batch sizes, sparsity, and precision when costs depend on secret data, while proving compliance with a declared leakage budget.
status: Frontier compiler target; optimization decisions themselves can become observable outputs.
why: Prevents the optimizer from revealing what the protocol hides.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Portable encrypted-state exit
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Move private application state between providers, parameter sets, and operator committees with a preservation proof and no plaintext export.
status: Design target; interchangeable primitive outputs are narrower than complete application-state portability.
why: Reduces infrastructure lock-in without weakening confidentiality.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Choudhuri et al. (2021), *Fluid MPC: Secure Multiparty Computation with Dynamic Participants*, ePrint 2020/754.

title: General invalid-witness-safe collaborative proving
open: Characterize and construct collaborative provers that preserve privacy on adversarially inconsistent witness shares for broad proof-system families.
status: Frontier following the 2025 analysis of malicious collaborative-SNARK security; a generic wrapper must not assume the distributed witness is valid.
why: Makes proof delegation safe against malicious contributors.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026.

title: Characterizing safe malicious-check elimination
open: Determine which collaborative prover computations can omit expensive malicious-consistency checks, and derive mechanically verifiable sufficient conditions.
status: Frontier extension; 2025 work establishes useful check-elimination results for several provers in the honest-majority setting.
why: Obtains malicious security without paying unnecessary generic-MPC overhead.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026.

title: Adaptively secure transparent collaborative proofs
open: Combine scalable transparent post-quantum collaborative proving with adaptive corruption of witness holders, prover randomness, and proof-state checkpoints.
status: Frontier combination; transparent post-quantum collaborative SNARKs already exist.
why: Protects distributed witnesses against compromise during long proving jobs.
key_works: Pappas, Papadopoulos, and Papamanthou (2026), *Code-based Scalable Collaborative SNARKs*, ePrint 2026/729.

title: Robust distributed-witness availability
open: Finish collaborative proofs despite permitted malicious dropout, using explicit redundancy or honest-majority assumptions and without exposing the witness.
status: Design target; collaborative proof generation and guaranteed proof completion are different properties.
why: Prevents a prover from holding completed private work hostage.
key_works: Ozdemir and Boneh (2022), *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs*; Liu et al. (2025), *Scalable Collaborative zk-SNARK and Its Application to Fully Distributed Proof Delegation*, ePrint 2024/940.

title: Physical-network costs of collaborative IVC
open: Preserve low incremental communication when ideal broadcast is replaced by authenticated WAN dissemination, including failures and proof publication.
status: Frontier implementation question; the 2026 collaborative-IVC result assumes a broadcast channel for its constant per-party per-step communication overhead.
why: Converts abstract communication gains into real bandwidth savings.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410.

title: Private proof continuation across committees
open: Transfer a running incremental proof and its secret state to a new committee while preserving soundness, witness privacy, and a unique authorized continuation.
status: Design target combining collaborative IVC with dynamic participation.
why: Enables proving services that outlive individual operators.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410; David, Mondal, and Satish (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Assumption-diverse private MSM outsourcing
open: Match efficient encrypted multi-scalar multiplication under alternative well-studied assumptions, retaining low client work and protection of statements, witnesses, and proofs.
status: Frontier extension; single-server private outsourcing already supports important SNARK families using LPN-based encrypted MSM.
why: Avoids concentrating private proof delegation on one assumption family.
key_works: Abbaszadeh, Hafezi, Katz, and Meiklejohn (2025/2026), *Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113.

title: WAN scaling for irregular collaborative proofs
open: Obtain strong distributed speedups for proofs with irregular dependencies, shared memory, and nonuniform witness access rather than only conveniently partitioned workloads.
status: Frontier workload extension; scalable distributed proof delegation provides a baseline.
why: Extends collaborative proving to realistic software and stateful applications.
key_works: Liu et al. (2025), *Scalable Collaborative zk-SNARK and Its Application to Fully Distributed Proof Delegation*, ePrint 2024/940.

title: Energy-efficient private proof delegation
open: Demonstrate at least 20× lower client energy for private proof generation while reporting server energy, network energy, preprocessing, and failure recovery.
status: Proposed measurement target; existing single-server outsourcing reports up to 18× client-computation reduction, not this complete energy result.
why: Makes proof generation usable on mobile and embedded clients.
key_works: Abbaszadeh et al. (2025/2026), *Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113.

title: Erasure-free quadratic asynchronous DKG
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Obtain constant-round, quadratic-communication asynchronous DKG from plain setup while eliminating secure erasures and preserving strong adaptive security.
status: Frontier combination; the 2026 quadratic plain-setup result assumes erasures, while erasure-free adaptive UC DKG exists in other settings.
why: Removes a difficult operational assumption without surrendering scalability.
key_works: Abraham, Bacho, and Stern (2026), *Quadratic Asynchronous DKG from Plain Setup*, ePrint 2026/1159; Ek et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/457.

title: One-round DKG without application-dangerous key bias
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Characterize when one-round additive key-shift freedom is harmless, and achieve stronger unbiasedness where applications require it without restoring expensive interaction.
status: Frontier tradeoff; Janus distinguishes a one-round key-shift-permitting variant from two-round unbiased key generation.
why: Prevents an efficient DKG variant from violating a downstream application’s assumptions.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Erasure-free DKG with compact public blame
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Combine erasure-free adaptive security, proactive refresh, and compact transferable blame at performance comparable to efficient erasure-assuming constructions.
status: Frontier combination; Janus reports 259-byte public blame certificates and refresh, while erasure-free UC constructions provide another frontier point.
why: Makes accountability independent of unverifiable deletion.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892; Ek et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/457.

title: Thousand-party adaptive DKG under active WAN faults
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Demonstrate adaptive DKG for at least 1,000 geographically distributed participants under Byzantine behavior, heterogeneous bandwidth, and restarts, reporting tail latency.
status: Proposed evidence target; Janus reports experiments through 512 nodes and approximately 310 ms for a sixteen-node intercontinental configuration.
why: Tests whether large committees remain deployable under attack.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Large post-quantum DKG with bounded pessimistic overhead
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Scale lattice-based asynchronous DKG to thousands of nodes while keeping Byzantine-path costs close to optimistic costs.
status: Proposed frontier target; LADKG reports optimistic completion in 45 seconds for 121 AWS nodes.
why: Makes post-quantum committees practical beyond small deployments.

title: Total-cost YOSO MPC
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers

subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: Obtain efficient update algorithms for general-access VSS when the policy changes, with costs tied to the policy delta rather than its complete monotone representation.
status: Frontier extension; computational VSS for general access structures is already a construction topic with positive results.
why: Supports organizational restructuring without wholesale resharing.

title: Packed gadgets robust to probes and faults
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers

title: Lower-cost dynamic-committee guaranteed output

status: Frontier; Rumors MPC gives strong guarantees with high polynomial communication costs.
why: Makes frequent operator replacement affordable.

title: Cross-protocol mobile-corruption budgets
open: Define one corruption budget across DKG, MPC, threshold decryption, and collaborative proving when these components refresh at different times.
status: Frontier composition question; asynchronous proactive models show why informal global-epoch accounting is insufficient.
why: Prevents individually valid refresh policies from failing in combination.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Minimal-overlap private committee transfer
open: Characterize and implement private state transfer between minimally overlapping committees with public correctness and explicit output-delivery conditions.
status: Frontier refinement of dynamic MPC; feasible overlap depends on communication, corruption, and surviving-state assumptions.
why: Allows genuine replacement of the original operators.
key_works: David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Proactive security with imperfect cloud erasure
open: Quantify guarantees when shares may survive in snapshots, swap, backups, crash dumps, or caches, and validate operational erasure procedures against that model.
status: Evidence gap; secure-erasure assumptions are explicit in efficient adaptive DKG, but malicious machines cannot cryptographically prove they retained no copy.

key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Refresh while serving concurrent requests

status: Design target; refresh protocols need additional concurrency and transactional semantics in a continuously available service.
why: Eliminates maintenance outages without weakening proactive privacy.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018; Li et al. (2026), *PUFF*, ePrint 2026/509.

title: Recovery guarantees with delayed compromise detection

status: Frontier modeling target; corruption-count bounds do not directly describe real incident-detection processes.
why: Makes proactive parameters meaningful for operations teams.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), *On the (Im)possibility of Asynchronous Proactive Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Empirical compromise-process models
open: Measure compromise duration, correlated breaches, repair time, and operator churn sufficiently well to evaluate proactive security under realistic distributions.
status: Evidence gap; formal mobile-adversary models provide hypotheses rather than empirical failure distributions.
why: Connects committee size and refresh frequency to actual risk.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018; Li et al. (2026), *PUFF*, ePrint 2026/509.

title: Durable, exactly-once private admission
open: Bind a client request to one durable execution and one authorized result across retries, coordinator crashes, and reconnection, without revealing its private input.
status: Design target; Dumbo-MPC already supplies robust asynchronous MPC-as-a-service foundations, but admission durability is an application-layer obligation.
why: Prevents duplicate private work and ambiguous completion.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC: Efficient Fully Asynchronous MPC with Optimal Resilience*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Non-reusable preprocessing across crashes
open: Prevent reuse of triples, masks, nonces, and proof randomness after rollback, migration, retries, and concurrent allocation, with auditable allocation metadata.
status: Engineering target; practical concurrency vulnerabilities show why protocol-state discipline matters.
why: Stops recovery from causing catastrophic secret reuse.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ: On the Practical Security of Malicious MPC Implementations*, ePrint 2025/789.

title: Multi-provider preemptible MPC
open: Extend preemption-tolerant MPC to heterogeneous cloud providers while preserving corruption assumptions during replacement and accounting for private state-transfer costs.
status: Frontier extension; ThriftyMPC already studies and implements spot-instance tolerance, so basic preemption support is not the gap.
why: Combines lower infrastructure costs with genuine operator diversity.

title: Verifiable preprocessing supply chains

status: Design target; efficient preprocessing exists, but a composable outsourced supply chain is a stronger service.
why: Separates expensive offline computation from online operation.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521; Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Multi-tenant cryptographic runtime isolation
open: Prove isolation among jobs sharing committees, accelerators, caches, preprocessing pools, and proof infrastructure, including concurrent malicious tenants.
status: Design target; primitive-level malicious security does not automatically protect a shared runtime.
why: Enables economical infrastructure without cross-customer leakage.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ*, ePrint 2025/789; De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*.

title: Privacy-preserving operational observability
open: Diagnose stalls, invalid shares, and resource exhaustion without logging reconstructable shares, witnesses, sensitive addresses, or private program behavior.
status: Engineering target; current runtime attacks and benchmarking tools motivate explicit safe telemetry.
why: Makes secure systems operable without disabling privacy during debugging.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Koch, Rotaru, and Rechberger (2025), *b4M: Holistic Benchmarking for MPC*, ePrint 2025/1106.

title: Resource-bounded private checkpointing
open: Checkpoint large MPC/FHE jobs with bounded memory and storage overhead while preserving consumed-randomness state, authorization, and proof continuity.
status: Design combination; incremental proving and preemption-tolerant MPC supply components, not arbitrary cross-stack checkpoint semantics.
why: Makes long-running private jobs recoverable on ordinary infrastructure.

title: Private cancellation with explicit completion semantics

status: Design target; cryptographic protocol abort and application cancellation are not equivalent.
why: Gives clients reliable control over long-lived private work.

status: Design combination; identification and continued progress are distinct guarantees.

status: Design target; correctness and eventual termination do not by themselves give resource-competitive behavior.

key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

open: Translate super-rushing security assumptions into machine-checkable requirements for event loops, pipelining, batching, and message handlers.

status: Frontier extension; existing work supplies efficient schemes for selected close-to-optimal constructions.
why: Turns combinatorial deterrence guarantees into practical protocols.

title: Bounding economically useful early-output advantage
open: Quantify and minimize the advantage from learning an output before honest parties when the value depends on timing and cannot necessarily be restored by later payment.

status: Frontier combination; standard-compatible threshold ML-DSA and FROST-like lattice constructions represent different design points.
