key_works: Bienstock et al. (2025/2026), *Quorus*, ePrint 2025/1163; Borin et al. (2026), *Hermine: An Efficient Lattice-based FROST-like Threshold Signature*, ePrint 2026/419.

title: Recovery without a custody superuser
open: Replace lost devices or operators through distributed recovery that cannot bypass ordinary authorization and produces verifiable recovery evidence.
status: Design target; the recovery authority must be included in the threshold service’s trust model.
why: Prevents emergency recovery from becoming the easiest takeover path.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Cross-domain authorization binding
open: Prevent authorizations and signing shares for one tenant, chain, protocol version, or transaction class from being replayed in another.
status: Engineering target; application context must be completely bound into signing and approval semantics.
why: Stops valid cryptography from authorizing the wrong action.
key_works: Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067; Baecker et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1950.

title: Censorship-resistant signing coordinators
open: Route authorized signing requests around malicious coordinators without duplicate execution, nonce misuse, or disclosure of private transaction metadata.
status: Design target; efficient signing and identifiable abort do not alone provide robust request routing.
why: Removes centralized availability from distributed custody.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2025/2026), *Fully Adaptive FROST with Identifiable Aborts from AOMDL*, ePrint 2025/1950.

title: Evidence of independent share control
open: Produce useful evidence that signing shares and recovery authority occupy genuinely separate administrative domains without exposing sensitive operational details.
status: Evidence target; a cryptographic threshold is not proof of independent ownership or infrastructure.
why: Makes custody decentralization measurable rather than nominal.
key_works: NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, IR 8214C.

title: Censorship-auditable sealed-bid clearing
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Prove correct clearing and inclusion of all timely accepted bids while hiding losing bids and preserving the declared output-delivery guarantee.
status: Design combination; robust MPC and private auctions exist, but correctness over a selectively chosen bid set is insufficient.
why: Prevents invisible bid suppression.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705; Baum, David, and Frederiksen (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283.

title: Post-quantum weighted, label-free batch decryption
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Achieve weighted batch threshold encryption without epoch labels or encryption-time indices, with compact per-party communication and post-quantum security.
status: Frontier combination; 2026 weighted constructions achieve strong compactness using bilinear-group assumptions.
why: Supports private transaction ordering without classical pairing dependencies.
key_works: Frolov, Partap, Resnick, and Tas (2026), *Weighted Batch Threshold Encryption with Efficient DKG*, ePrint 2026/2053.

title: Small batch-decryption keys without positional restrictions
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Reduce committee secret-key storage while preserving unrestricted placement of pending ciphertexts and efficient verifiable batch decryption.
status: Frontier tradeoff; Simple BTE reduces key size through a variant that restricts permissible ciphertext positions.
why: Avoids trading censorship resistance for storage efficiency.
key_works: Policharla (2026), *A Simple Batched Threshold Encryption Scheme*, ePrint 2026/760.

title: Provable private order cancellation
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Support encrypted-order cancellation and replacement with unambiguous ordering relative to admission and clearing, without revealing order content or permitting retroactive cancellation.
status: Design target; private matching does not automatically establish cancellation semantics.
why: Makes confidential markets operationally usable.
key_works: Baum, David, and Frederiksen (2021), *P2DEX: Privacy-Preserving Decentralized Cryptocurrency Exchange*, ePrint 2021/283.

title: Private cross-venue atomic settlement
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Settle privately matched trades across heterogeneous ledgers or custody systems without revealing orders to one settlement agent or assuming synchronized finality.
status: Design combination; private matching and confidential transfers solve different parts of settlement.
why: Extends private markets beyond isolated venues.
key_works: Baum et al. (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283; Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850.

title: Private collateral without double commitment
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Prove hidden orders are collateralized and not simultaneously pledged elsewhere, while revealing neither total holdings nor trading strategy.
status: Design target; confidential balances and valid transfers do not automatically establish global exclusivity of commitments.
why: Prevents private markets from depending on trusted credit exposure.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces: Confidential Token Transfers via MPC and CoSNARKs*, ePrint 2026/850.

title: Residual manipulation after encrypted ordering
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Characterize and reduce profitable manipulation remaining after transaction encryption, including selective release, inclusion timing, post-decryption ordering, and coalition behavior.
status: Frontier mechanism question; encrypted mempools protect specified transaction information but do not automatically establish complete market fairness.
why: Measures the economic protection actually delivered.
key_works: Bormet et al. (2025/2026), *BEAST-MEV*, ePrint 2025/1419; Frolov et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2053.

title: Large robust and auditable sealed-bid auctions
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Clear 100,000 bids with malicious security, public correctness, and fault recovery within a declared latency budget, counting amortized preprocessing.
status: Proposed moonshot; Dumbo-MPC’s published 31-party example uses minutes of preparation for a 100-bidder Vickrey auction.
why: Enables private allocation at exchange or public-market scale.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Repeated-market output privacy
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Design matching and pricing rules whose repeated legitimate outputs reveal acceptably little about losing bids, inventory, reserve prices, and strategies.
status: Frontier mechanism question; cryptographic execution privacy does not hide information intentionally released by the market rule.
why: Preserves economic privacy beyond encrypting the order book.
key_works: Baum et al. (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283; Friolo et al. (2022), arXiv:2207.10780.

title: Fast general private execution without hardware trust
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Raise sustained publicly auditable, EVM-compatible confidential execution to at least 500 transactions/second on declared workloads without TEEs.
status: Proposed performance target; gcVM reports 83 confidential transactions/second, while 500 is a projection rather than its measured result.
why: Makes general private applications practical beyond simple transfers.
key_works: Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM: Publicly Auditable MPC via Garbled Circuits with Applications to Private EVM-Compatible Computation*, ePrint 2026/170.

title: Private-state data availability
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Guarantee sufficient valid shares remain recoverable for authorized continuation without publishing private state or trusting one archive.
status: Design target; a valid state-transition proof does not establish continued availability of the state it commits to.
why: Prevents valid private contracts from becoming permanently frozen.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Alhaddad et al. (2025), *Haven++*, DOI:10.62056/a0qj5w7sf.

title: Recovering the unique finalized private state
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Restore the last finalized private state after failures, with proof of commitment consistency and protection against stale or forked recovery snapshots.
status: Design target; confidential-state commitments and committee reconfiguration require an explicit recovery composition.
why: Makes private contracts durable across operational incidents.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Atomic private calls across committees
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Execute transactions spanning private state controlled by different committees without leaking intermediate values, weakening either trust policy, or leaving partial commits.
status: Frontier system combination; a secure single-committee private state machine does not supply arbitrary cross-committee atomicity.
why: Enables composable private applications rather than silos.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Conflict-private transaction concurrency
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Parallelize transactions over secret state with provable serializability while hiding which records, accounts, or contracts conflict.
status: Design frontier beyond correct sequential private execution.
why: Improves throughput without revealing the application’s access graph.
key_works: Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM*, ePrint 2026/170; Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039.

title: Verifiable private upgrades
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Upgrade code and private-state representations with proofs of authorization, invariant preservation, and preservation of existing user rights.
status: Design target; proving execution of fixed code is weaker than proving a safe change to that code.
why: Permits repair without unrestricted administrative power.
key_works: Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM*, ePrint 2026/170; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Thin-client private applications without trusted gateways
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Let constrained clients authenticate inputs and verify general private-state transitions without downloading private state, constructing large witnesses, or trusting a privileged relay.
status: Design extension; lightweight clients exist for specialized confidential transfers, but general application support is broader.
why: Makes private applications accessible from ordinary devices.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434.

title: Ten-thousand-transition private-state services
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Sustain 10,000 publicly verifiable private state transitions/second on a specified WAN committee while measuring active-fault recovery and including proof generation.
status: Proposed moonshot; Merces reports over 300 confidential transfers/second in its benchmark configuration.
why: Supports high-volume private shared-state applications.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces: Confidential Token Transfers via MPC and CoSNARKs*, ePrint 2026/850.

title: Bounded emergency governance for private services
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Make committee replacement, fee changes, policy updates, and emergency actions verifiably authorized with explicit limits on what emergency powers can reveal or override.
status: Design target; cryptographic execution does not automatically constrain governance.
why: Prevents administrators from undoing trust minimization.
key_works: Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067; Garg et al. (2025), *Threshold Anonymous Credentials with Silent Setup*, ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Compact post-quantum verifiable shuffles
open: Match modern compact ElGamal-shuffle proof sizes and practical prover performance under post-quantum assumptions.
status: Frontier; the 2026 ElGamal construction reports a 2.6 KiB proof for \(2^{20}\) ciphertexts under its structured-setup model.
why: Preserves publicly auditable mixing after quantum migration.
key_works: Xue, Lu, and Au (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles for ElGamal Ciphertexts*, ePrint 2026/805.

title: Transparent compact shuffle proofs
open: Remove structured setup from compact verifiable shuffles while retaining small proofs and near-linear practical proving work.
status: Frontier tradeoff; the cited logarithmic-size shuffle uses an updatable structured reference string.
why: Reduces setup dependencies in auditable mixnets.
key_works: Xue, Lu, and Au (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles for ElGamal Ciphertexts*, ePrint 2026/805.

title: Auditable mixing with traffic-analysis guarantees
open: Compose verified shuffling with quantified anonymity under realistic timing, volume, retries, and partial network observation.
status: Design combination; shuffle correctness and Loopix-style traffic defenses address different attack surfaces.
why: A correct permutation does not hide correlations in surrounding traffic.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *The Loopix Anonymity System*, arXiv:1703.00536; Xue et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/805.

title: Anonymous accountability for dropped packets
open: Attribute malicious dropping or malformed forwarding without revealing sender–receiver links, under explicit assumptions distinguishing relay behavior from network loss.
status: Frontier combination; mixing and public blame need a shared leakage and delivery model.
why: Improves availability without sacrificing anonymity during disputes.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

title: Proactive mixnet keys with historical anonymity
open: Refresh distributed relay authority so gradual compromise does not reveal historical communication links beyond an explicit leakage model.
status: Frontier lifecycle combination of anonymous communication and proactive sharing.
why: Protects archived traffic against sequential operator compromise.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Fast robust mixing including preparation
open: Reduce total maliciously secure asynchronous mixing cost by two orders of magnitude on a reproduced workload, including adverse-path preprocessing.
status: Proposed moonshot; Dumbo-MPC reports 10–36 minutes of preparation for its 31-party, \(2^{10}\)-input mixing example.
why: Makes robust private communication responsive.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Adaptive cover traffic with certified leakage
open: Adapt cover traffic to load, battery, bandwidth, and latency constraints while bounding the information revealed by the adaptation.
status: Frontier extension; fixed traffic-shaping mechanisms provide a baseline, not a free adaptive optimization.
why: Reduces anonymity costs without silently discarding anonymity.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *The Loopix Anonymity System*, arXiv:1703.00536.

title: Anonymous authenticated private RPC
open: Hide which user invokes which MPC/FHE service while supporting credentials, quotas, reliable responses, and abuse handling.
status: Design combination; mixnets, credentials, and private computation have different metadata interfaces.
why: Protects service-use metadata as well as input content.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344.

title: Adversarial mixnet replay datasets
open: Publish privacy-respecting traces and replay tools covering churn, congestion, heterogeneous clients, packet dropping, and adaptive observation.
status: Evidence gap; individual system evaluations are not a common adversarial benchmark.
why: Makes availability and anonymity claims comparable.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Xue et al. (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles*, ePrint 2026/805.

title: Malicious updatable multiparty PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Preserve update-proportional computation and low online interaction while providing malicious security for large multiparty updatable PSI.
status: Frontier extension; the 2026 one-pass construction is semi-honest and has leader-dependent collusion guarantees.
why: Supports continuing collaboration among adversarial organizations.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), *Multi-Party Private Set Intersection with Optimal Online Round Complexity and Updatability*, ePrint 2026/1774.

title: Leader-independent update-efficient PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Remove privileged-leader assumptions from update-efficient multiparty PSI while retaining favorable communication and large-coalition resistance.
status: Frontier refinement; the cited updatable construction assumes an honest leader for its strongest collusion guarantee.
why: Avoids concentrating trust in the intersection coordinator.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1774.

title: Fast PSI updates secure against adaptive input selection
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Combine symmetric-key-heavy update efficiency, malicious security, deletion support, and protection against adaptively selected future updates.
status: Frontier combination; Liu et al. identify adaptive-update attacks and provide secure variants, so adaptive safety itself is not wholly unconstructed.
why: Prevents a long-lived PSI service from leaking through its update history.
key_works: Liu, Miao, Rosulek, Shi, and Wang (2026), *Updatable Private Set Intersection from Symmetric-Key Techniques*, ePrint 2026/438.

title: Enriched PSI without additional cardinality leakage
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Retain efficient malicious PSI-sum, circuit-PSI, and set-union functionality while hiding intersection size whenever it is not implied by the authorized output.
status: Frontier refinement; the 2026 shuffled-DOPRF approach explicitly permits additional intersection-cardinality leakage.
why: Protects sensitive relationship counts.
key_works: van Baarsen et al. (2026), *Maliciously Secure Shuffled Distributed OPRF with Applications to Private Set Operations*, ePrint 2026/2035.

title: Assumption-conservative post-quantum enriched PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Instantiate efficient malicious enriched set operations using well-analyzed post-quantum primitives with concrete reductions and parameters.
status: Frontier target; the 2026 shuffled-DOPRF work offers DDH and a plausibly post-quantum Dark-Matter-based variant.
why: Supports durable privacy for sensitive institutional linkage.
key_works: van Baarsen et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2035; Liu, Rosulek, and Trieu (2026), *Post-Quantum Private Set Intersection for Small Sets*, ePrint 2026/1985.

title: Low-bandwidth post-quantum small-set PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Reduce post-quantum small-set PSI communication to within 2× a matched classical baseline while retaining the stated security model.
status: Proposed moonshot; Liu–Rosulek–Trieu report as little as 1.67 KiB/item and a 16.7× communication penalty in their comparison.
why: Makes private contact and credential matching practical on mobile links.
key_works: Liu, Rosulek, and Trieu (2026), *Post-Quantum Private Set Intersection for Small Sets*, ePrint 2026/1985.

title: Output-sensitive fuzzy PSI on dense datasets
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Obtain efficient fuzzy matching without restrictive separation or density assumptions, with costs sensitive to unavoidable output size and explicit dimensional dependence.
status: Frontier; Paik–Seo replace separation with a bounded-collision condition rather than eliminating all structural assumptions.
why: Covers real clustered identifiers and embeddings.
key_works: Paik and Seo (2026), *Fuzzy Private Set Intersection from Density-Bounded Assumptions*, ePrint 2026/262.

title: Publicly auditable authenticated set operations
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Prove a private set-operation result came from authenticated committed snapshots and permitted updates, without revealing nonmatching elements.
status: Design combination of malicious set operations and authenticated-input computation.
why: Lets outsiders verify private linkage results.
key_works: van Baarsen et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2035; Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Billion-record private linkage under churn
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Demonstrate authenticated, maliciously secure, updateable set operations over billion-record datasets with recovery and explicit leakage, storage, and network budgets.
status: Proposed moonshot; the cited multiparty baseline evaluates sets through \(2^{20}\) items under a weaker threat model.
why: Supports industry-wide or national-scale private linkage.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1774; Liu et al. (2026), *Updatable Private Set Intersection from Symmetric-Key Techniques*, ePrint 2026/438.

title: Malicious private SQL with outsider verification
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Combine maliciously secure collaborative SQL with succinct proofs binding the query, authenticated input snapshots, and result while hiding intermediate relations.
status: Design frontier; Senate supplies malicious collaborative analytics, not automatically every public-audit requirement.
why: Makes private analytics independently checkable.
key_works: Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate: A Maliciously-Secure MPC Platform for Collaborative Analytics*, USENIX Security 2021.

title: Private query planning without selectivity leakage
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Optimize joins, indexes, partitioning, and pushdown without exposing sensitive cardinalities or selectivities beyond a negotiated leakage policy.
status: Frontier compiler target; Conclave demonstrates hybrid optimization benefits, but private cost estimation needs its own guarantees.
why: Prevents query planning from leaking protected data.
key_works: Volgushev et al. (2019), *Conclave: Secure Multi-Party Computation on Big Data*, arXiv:1902.06288.

title: Incrementally verifiable private materialized views
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Maintain secret-shared views with update-proportional work and incremental public proofs, including deletions and ownership changes.
status: Design combination; collaborative IVC supplies incremental proof machinery, while databases require additional update semantics.
why: Avoids complete recomputation after small changes.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410; Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*.

title: Private streaming joins with bounded state
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Execute authenticated streaming joins and windowed aggregates with bounded secret state, explicit late-data semantics, and verifiable completeness.
status: Design extension of private analytics and incremental verification; static-query correctness does not specify continuing stream semantics.
why: Enables private monitoring and operational analytics.
key_works: Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410.

title: Hardware-independent horizontal private analytics
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Match the useful scale of hardware-assisted private analytics while eliminating or substantially weakening TEE assumptions.
status: Frontier target; CoVault explicitly combines server-aided MPC and TEEs to scale within a datacenter.
why: Reduces reliance on a small set of hardware trust roots.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data*, USENIX Security 2025.

title: Malicious analytics under heterogeneous trust policies
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Execute a joint analysis when owners trust different operator subsets and corruption thresholds, preserving each owner’s policy rather than collapsing to the weakest one.
status: Frontier extension; heterogeneous-trust optimization already has precedents, but this stronger malicious-security combination requires explicit construction.
why: Supports institutions with incompatible governance requirements.
key_works: Volgushev et al. (2019), *Conclave*, arXiv:1902.06288; Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*.

title: Enforceable future-use restrictions after deletion
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Enforce deletion or consent withdrawal for future computation while explicitly excluding impossible promises to erase already learned outputs or maliciously retained plaintext.
status: Design target; meaningful deletion depends on key management, storage, and erasure assumptions.
why: Makes data-lifecycle privacy promises operationally precise.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Crash-consistent private database recovery
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Recover large shared databases without rolling back access control, privacy budgets, consumed randomness, or key epochs relative to the restored data snapshot.
status: Design target; data confidentiality alone does not establish consistency of all recovery metadata.
why: Prevents backup restoration from invalidating privacy.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*; Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ*, ePrint 2025/789.

title: Churn-tolerant publicly verifiable distributed RAM
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Extend publicly verifiable distributed oblivious RAM with efficient committee replacement, concurrency, and recovery while preserving hidden addresses.
status: Frontier extension; VDORAM already constructs and implements public verifiability with distributed obliviousness.
why: Supports realistic long-lived private programs.
key_works: Qi, Xu, Jia, and Cheng (2025/2026), *VDORAM: Towards a Random Access Machine with Both Public Verifiability and Distributed Obliviousness*, ePrint 2025/039.

title: Proactive private revocation with intermittent clients
open: Combine large-scale private revocation with changing authorities, proactive recovery, and intermittently connected holders while bounding stale-credential acceptance.
status: Frontier extension; decentralized real-time private revocation already reports subsecond operation over more than one billion credentials.
why: Makes anonymous authorization robust over long lifetimes.
key_works: Edalatnejad et al. (2026), *Do You Need a Receipt? Anonymous Credential Revocation at Continental Scale via Private Record Certification*, ePrint 2026/1189.

title: Silent-setup credentials beyond generic-group analysis
open: Obtain comparable threshold issuance, issuer hiding, constant-size showing, and dynamic verifier policies under alternative assumptions with concrete reductions.
status: Frontier extension; the cited silent-setup construction proves security in the generic group model.
why: Diversifies the foundations of decentralized identity.
key_works: Garg, Garg, Policharla, and Roberts (2025), *Threshold Anonymous Credentials with Silent Setup*, ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Practical post-quantum threshold issuer-hiding credentials
open: Combine post-quantum security, threshold issuance, issuer hiding, flexible policies, and mobile-scale showing costs.
status: Frontier combination; strong classical threshold-credential constructions establish useful baselines, not this complete post-quantum package.
why: Protects identity privacy and authenticity over decades.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Unlinkable stateful entitlements
open: Enforce spending limits, one-time rights, or per-user quotas across multiple verifiers without creating a globally linkable user identifier.
status: Design frontier; authenticating an unlinkable credential does not itself synchronize consumption of its rights.
why: Enables anonymous access to scarce services.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189.

title: Credential issuance from authenticated private evidence
open: Issue credentials from TLS-derived or jointly computed evidence while hiding unnecessary source data from issuers and preserving provenance into later showings.
status: Design combination; authenticated input transfer and threshold credentials supply separate components.
why: Avoids disclosing complete records to obtain a minimal credential.
key_works: Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434; Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Anonymous migration across issuer committees
open: Replace issuer committees without forcing holders to reveal identities, surrender unlinkability, or reissue every credential from original evidence.
status: Design target; threshold issuance and dynamic participation do not automatically provide holder-preserving migration.
why: Prevents permanent dependence on initial issuers.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Non-linkable evidence of issuer misconduct
open: Prove unauthorized, conflicting, or malformed issuance without identifying honest holders or exposing their authentication histories.
status: Frontier combination of anonymous credentials and public accountability.
why: Makes issuers answerable without making users traceable.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

title: Credential recovery without universal impersonation
open: Restore lost credentials through distributed recovery that cannot silently impersonate all holders or link identities across services.
status: Design target; holder recovery introduces authority beyond ordinary issuance and showing.
why: Reconciles usable identity with resistance to centralized takeover.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; NIST (2026), IR 8214C.

title: Adversarial credential-lifecycle benchmarks
open: Benchmark issuance, revocation bursts, authority churn, mobile constraints, and longitudinal linkage attacks together at large population scale.
status: Evidence gap; billion-credential revocation performance already exists, but it does not certify an entire credential ecosystem.
why: Measures the privacy and availability holders experience.
key_works: Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189; Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Distributed-witness proofs of private training
open: Prove an agreed training procedure over multiple private datasets without centralizing either the data or the complete training witness.
status: Frontier combination; zkDL proves training, while collaborative proving protects distributed witnesses.
why: Makes collaborative model production independently auditable.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Deep Learning Training*, ePrint 2023/1174; Pappas et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/729.

title: Verifiable private federated LoRA
open: Extend efficient LoRA training proofs to federated private datasets with malicious contributors, authenticated aggregation, and recoverable distributed proving.
status: Frontier extension; VeriLoRA already proves LoRA fine-tuning, so basic verifiable fine-tuning is not open.
why: Enables auditable adaptation of shared models without pooling sensitive data.
key_works: Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models with Verifiable Security via Zero-Knowledge Proofs*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Poisoning resistance beyond valid update constraints
open: Bound damage from updates that satisfy all enforced norm, range, and formatting constraints while preserving honest-update privacy.
status: Frontier; RoFL and EIFFeL enforce integrity predicates, but satisfying a predicate is not equivalent to semantic harmlessness.
why: Prevents privacy protections from hiding effective model poisoning.
key_works: Lycklama et al. (2023), *RoFL: Robustness of Secure Federated Learning*, arXiv:2107.03311; Roy Chowdhury et al. (2022), *EIFFeL*, arXiv:2112.12727.

title: Authenticated private training examples
open: Prove training examples originate from authorized sources and satisfy provenance requirements without exposing them or conflating authenticity with correct labeling.
status: Design combination; authenticated MPC and training proofs supply different guarantees.
why: Reduces fabricated-data and unauthorized-data attacks.
key_works: Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648; Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174.

title: Verifiable training under numerical nondeterminism
open: Certify allowed training behavior across different accelerators and numerical schedules without requiring bit-identical execution or permitting arbitrary model drift.
status: Frontier extension; exact execution proofs need a carefully specified relation when production training is numerically nondeterministic.
why: Makes training verification compatible with real distributed ML.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Dropout-robust aggregation with honest privacy accounting
open: Combine malicious-update validation, dropout recovery, unbiased privacy noise, and accounting that remains valid when participants strategically abort.
status: Frontier combination; robust private aggregation and abort-aware differential privacy address separate portions.
why: Keeps training privacy valid under realistic participation failures.
key_works: Roy Chowdhury et al. (2022), *EIFFeL*, arXiv:2112.12727; Meisingseth (2026), ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Proving training-data inclusion without revealing records
open: Prove that all required accepted records or contributions were used according to the training policy, rather than merely proving training on an operator-selected subset.
status: Design target; valid training execution does not establish completeness of the selected dataset.
why: Prevents silent omission and selective model construction.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Dutta et al. (2024), ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Private model-update ratchets
open: Bind each deployed model to authorized training or fine-tuning history and prevent rollback to disallowed versions while keeping model parameters private.
status: Design combination; training and inference proofs do not automatically enforce deployment history.
why: Makes model governance auditable rather than discretionary.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Sun, Li, and Zhang (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Private verifiable training within tenfold cost
open: Demonstrate complete private, maliciously secure, publicly verifiable training within 10× a declared plaintext training baseline, including proof and communication costs.
status: Proposed moonshot; specialized training proofs and secure learning systems do not establish this combined ratio.
why: Makes trustworthy collaborative training economically practical.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Both-sided malicious security for verifiable large-model inference
open: Combine client-input privacy, model privacy, malicious security for both sides, and proof of authorized-model execution at useful large-transformer latency.
status: Frontier combination; private inference, malicious-client protection, and large-model proofs have separate strong results.
why: Removes trust in both the client and model operator.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE*, ePrint 2021/1040; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*.

title: Inference proofs with numerical fidelity
open: Prove that quantization, truncation, polynomial approximations, and encrypted arithmetic preserve a stated error or task-quality guarantee relative to the authorized reference model.
status: Frontier; correct cryptographic execution and acceptable model approximation are different claims.
why: Prevents performance optimizations from silently changing the service.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Private, verifiable autoregressive state
open: Protect prompts, generated-token state, and caches across long conversations while proving every continuation and supporting crash recovery.
status: Design extension; private transformer inference and large-model proofs do not automatically provide durable conversational state.
why: Enables private assistants rather than isolated forward passes.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Hiding adaptive model routing and sequence structure
open: Bound leakage from sequence lengths, early exits, mixture-of-experts routing, sparsity, and adaptive batching in private verifiable inference.
status: Frontier deployment target; hiding numerical inputs does not automatically hide execution structure.
why: Protects metadata that may reveal user intent or content.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Verifiable private retrieval-augmented generation
open: Prove authorized retrieval from a committed private corpus and correct use of retrieved records in inference while hiding queries, access patterns, and confidential model parameters.
status: Design combination; distributed oblivious RAM and model proofs provide separate building blocks.
why: Extends private inference to systems grounded in private databases.
key_works: Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Private inference bound to live model policy
open: Bind each result to an authorized model version, permitted adapter set, and current access policy, including concurrent updates and retries.
status: Design target; a valid inference proof does not by itself establish freshness or authorization of the model.
why: Prevents model substitution and stale-model execution.
key_works: Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109; Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Output-policy defenses against model extraction
open: Enforce private query policies that mitigate extraction and membership inference through legitimate outputs without revealing user queries to a trusted monitor.
status: Frontier service problem; malicious-client security prevents protocol deviations but does not eliminate all black-box extraction.
why: Protects both model assets and training-data privacy.
key_works: Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE: Secure Inference Resilient to Malicious Clients*, ePrint 2021/1040.

title: Jointly private and verifiable inference within tenfold cost
open: Achieve less than 10× total overhead for a declared large-model workload with input privacy, model privacy, malicious security, and verifiable execution simultaneously.
status: Proposed moonshot; isolated inference or proof-kernel timings do not establish this joint-property benchmark.
why: Makes trust-minimized ML competitive as a routine service.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*; Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE*; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*.

title: Selective-failure-resistant hybrid inference
open: Prevent malicious ciphertexts, malformed intermediate values, or client-controlled nonlinear steps from creating selective-failure leakage in hybrid HE–MPC inference.
status: Frontier hardening target; malicious-client inference attacks demonstrate that semi-honest hybrid reasoning is insufficient.
why: Protects model and input privacy under active protocol manipulation.
key_works: Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE*, ePrint 2021/1040; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Certified noise under changing distributed authority
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Preserve certified noise distributions across threshold generation, committee refresh, malicious dropout, and private output release.
status: Frontier combination; Noisette already certifies broad discrete and continuous noise mechanisms, including floating-point privacy effects.
why: Removes trusted noise generation from long-lived private services.
key_works: Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette: Certifying Differential Privacy Mechanisms Efficiently*, ePrint 2026/074.

title: Tight privacy composition under adaptive abort-and-retry
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Derive tight lifetime privacy bounds for repeated executions in which adversaries adaptively abort, retry, and select which outputs become visible.
status: Frontier extension; 2026 abort analysis gives important single-execution and functionality-level distinctions.
why: Prevents repeated rejection from biasing private releases.
key_works: Meisingseth (2026), *On Aborts in Differential Privacy*, ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Fork-resistant distributed privacy budgets
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Enforce one privacy accountant across concurrent queries, retries, committee replacement, and restored backups, preventing budget reset or double spending.
status: Design target; secure aggregation does not automatically provide durable global release governance.
why: Keeps lifetime privacy promises valid after failures.
key_works: Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio: Private, Robust, and Scalable Computation of Aggregate Statistics*, NSDI 2017; Meisingseth (2026), ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Private heterogeneous privacy accounting
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Enforce contributor-specific privacy limits without revealing the limits, participation patterns, or which contributor caused rejection.
status: Frontier system combination of distributed aggregation and private policy enforcement.
why: Supports collaborations whose members require different protection levels.
key_works: Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio*; Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074.

title: Hidden sensitivity and cohort certificates
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Certify sensitivity bounds, clipping rules, cohort sizes, and accounting parameters while hiding protected population statistics.
status: Frontier; correct noise sampling does not justify every parameter supplied to the mechanism.
why: Prevents proofs from certifying incorrectly parameterized privacy claims.
key_works: Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074; Bontekoe, Asghar, and Turkmen (2024), ePrint 2024/1042.

title: Authenticated sampling against Sybil participants
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Preserve useful privacy and utility when contributors strategically duplicate identities, join, leave, or submit correlated records, using private eligibility evidence where appropriate.
status: Frontier combination; authenticated-input verifiable DP exists, but participation manipulation needs explicit treatment.
why: Prevents privacy guarantees from assuming an unrealistically honest population.
key_works: Bontekoe, Asghar, and Turkmen (2024), *Efficient Verifiable Differential Privacy with Input Authenticity in the Local and Shuffle Model*, ePrint 2024/1042.

title: Auditable robust statistics without exposing outliers
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Certify robust estimators, rejection rules, randomness, and approximation error while hiding outliers and rejected contributors.
status: Design combination; robust private aggregation and certified noise mechanisms address different layers.
why: Makes private statistical services resilient to bad data.
key_works: Lycklama et al. (2023), *RoFL*, arXiv:2107.03311; Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074.

title: Public auditing without participation leakage
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Publish verifiable aggregate results without revealing whether a particular person participated through proofs, timing, batch failures, or admission records.
status: Design target; public auditability and private aggregation require one participation-leakage definition.
why: Protects the fact of participation, not only submitted values.
key_works: Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio*; Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Joint privacy–utility–trust–cost frontiers
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Publish reproducible Pareto frontiers over privacy loss, statistical accuracy, corruption assumptions, latency, communication, and energy for representative workloads.
status: Evidence gap; privacy mechanisms and cryptographic benchmarks typically optimize different objective sets.
why: Helps users select meaningful guarantees rather than isolated records.
key_works: Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074; Koch et al. (2025), *b4M*, ePrint 2025/1106.

title: Mechanically verified concurrent MPC runtimes
open: Verify message scheduling, MAC checking, shared-state access, and concurrent job execution against the malicious-security proof.
status: Engineering frontier; practical SPDZ attacks demonstrate vulnerabilities at the concurrency boundary.
why: Makes protocol security survive parallel execution.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ: On the Practical Security of Malicious MPC Implementations*, ePrint 2025/789.

title: Verified delayed-consistency-check optimization
open: Automatically move, batch, or delay checks using proved dependency conditions, rejecting transformations that expose unchecked adversarial values unsafely.
status: Frontier response to 2026 attacks and fixes; the repaired instances themselves are not listed as still broken.
why: Preserves performance optimization without recurring security mistakes.
key_works: Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), *When Trying to Catch Cheaters Breaks the MPC: Breaking and Fixing Delayed Consistency Checks in Trident, Fantastic Four, SWIFT, and Quad*, ePrint 2026/234.

title: Proof-carrying cryptographic parameters
open: Attach machine-checkable evidence to parameter choices covering security level, noise, proof soundness, packing, and allowed conversions across the stack.
status: Design target; independently plausible defaults need not form a safe combined configuration.
why: Prevents configuration errors from invalidating mathematical guarantees.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956; Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Leakage-certified accelerator kernels
open: Validate MPC, FHE, and proof accelerators against explicit cache, memory-access, contention, and multi-tenant side-channel models.
status: Experimental frontier; cryptographic privacy does not automatically imply accelerator-level noninterference.
why: Prevents hardware speedups from reopening plaintext leakage channels.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Cross-platform arithmetic equivalence
open: Automatically verify equivalence of CPU and accelerator cryptographic kernels, including lazy reduction, vectorization, overflow, decomposition, and exceptional inputs.
status: Engineering target; proof-friendly arithmetic representations expose specific translation obligations.
why: Allows implementation portability without changing ciphertext semantics.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956; Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots*.

title: Leakage-certified data-dependent control flow
open: Automatically select oblivious execution, padding, private branching, or explicit declassification while proving a user-declared confidentiality contract.
status: Frontier compiler target; general MPC frameworks provide programming support, not automatic certification of every application leakage choice.
why: Reduces dependence on manual cryptographic code review.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Adversarial cross-library interoperability
open: Make independent MPC, FHE, and proof implementations interoperate under malformed messages, version mismatch, aborted sessions, and incompatible parameters.
status: Engineering target; successful primitive test vectors are narrower than malicious-path interoperability.
why: Enables implementation diversity without creating new protocol seams.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Safe fallback when hardware trust fails
open: Design hybrid TEE–MPC services with explicit residual guarantees and a demonstrated recovery path when one hardware trust root fails.
status: Frontier architecture question; hardware-assisted scalability does not by itself provide assumption-failure recovery.
why: Uses hardware performance without treating hardware trust as absolute.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data*, USENIX Security 2025.

title: Source-to-proof semantic binding
open: Verify that deployed binaries, compiled MPC circuits, proof relations, and user-visible program versions represent the same authorized computation.
status: Design target; verifying a circuit does not establish that it faithfully implements the intended source program.
why: Closes a major gap between cryptographic correctness and application correctness.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521; Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039.

title: Security-normalized cross-stack benchmarks
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Compare systems after normalizing corruption model, output guarantee, setup, quantum assumptions, leakage, precision, and included lifecycle costs.
status: Evidence infrastructure target; b4M supplies benchmarking machinery, but cross-paradigm security normalization is broader.
why: Prevents weaker guarantees from masquerading as unexplained performance superiority.
key_works: Koch, Rotaru, and Rechberger (2025), *b4M: Holistic Benchmarking for MPC*, ePrint 2025/1106.

title: Shared adversarial lifecycle test suite
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Build reusable tests for malformed inputs, malicious shares, selective aborts, super-rushing, coordinator loss, rollback, churn, and recovery.
status: Evidence gap; published attacks and repairs provide concrete regression seeds, not a complete cross-system suite.
why: Makes security claims experimentally falsifiable.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), ePrint 2026/234; Ciampi et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1745.

title: Reproducible total energy and cost accounting
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Measure complete setup, refresh, preprocessing, computation, proving, communication, storage, and recovery costs on published hardware and workloads.
status: Evidence target; selected online-phase or kernel measurements do not establish service economics.
why: Identifies which trust-minimization combinations are sustainable.
key_works: Koch et al. (2025), *b4M*, ePrint 2025/1106; Inyangson et al. (2026), *ThriftyMPC*, ePrint 2026/977.

title: Corpus of cryptographic integration failures
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Create a structured corpus linking failures to violated assumptions, vulnerable interfaces, exploit prerequisites, repairs, and executable regressions.
status: Data target; recent implementation attacks and proof corrections supply initial cases.
why: Lets systems learn from recurring failures instead of rediscovering them.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), ePrint 2026/234; Peshawaria et al. (2025/2026), *Laminate*, ePrint 2025/2285.

title: Independent replication of frontier systems
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Reproduce major DKG, threshold-FHE, collaborative-proof, and private-state benchmarks on independently operated infrastructure while preserving their security models.
status: Evidence target; publication and available code do not establish independent replication.
why: Produces reliable records for future research and deployment.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057; Pappas et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/729; Escudero et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/850.

title: Machine-readable trust and guarantee manifests
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Standardize machine-checkable descriptions of setup authorities, thresholds, leakage, failure semantics, parameter dependencies, and permitted compositions, linked to concrete implementations.
status: Engineering infrastructure target; NIST’s reference-material process provides a foundation, not automatic whole-stack validation.
why: Makes a cross-linked problem census useful for selecting actual systems.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Sustainable maintenance and replication funding
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Measure maintenance and independent-audit needs, then evaluate funding mechanisms supporting multiyear compatibility, security fixes, and replication rather than only initial constructions.
status: Funding hypothesis, not a claim that funding is absent; the VERIFHE project is one documented funded effort.
why: Keeps foundational software trustworthy after its initial research release.
key_works: European Commission (2026), *VERIFHE: An Open-Source Library for Verifiable Fully Homomorphic Encryption for Trustworthy Machine Learning*, grant 101287502, DOI:10.3030/101287502.

title: Procurement evidence for actual trust reduction
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Develop testable procurement criteria separating mathematical thresholds from operator independence, centralized recovery, hardware assumptions, and unverified availability claims.
status: Governance and evidence target; NIST’s threshold call collects reference material and is not certification of every deployment.
why: Allows institutions to purchase demonstrated trust reduction rather than labels.
key_works: NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, IR 8214C.

title: Continuously corrected open-problem registry
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Maintain a versioned registry distinguishing established open questions, proposed targets, solved variants, impossibility boundaries, unverified claims, and superseding results.
status: Infrastructure target; recent results repeatedly invalidate broad older labels such as “compact multi-key FHE” or “private large-scale revocation is missing.”
why: Makes a million-problem census cumulative instead of duplicative or stale.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Abraham et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1159; Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189.
